## Teaching philosophy {#philosophy}

I am early in my academic teaching career, so my approach is practical and comes from what
has worked in my tutoring and guest lecturing. It also draws on teaching in
high-responsibility settings outside academia, as an outdoor guide and certified ACA
sea-kayak instructor. In every setting, students learn more when they are thinking,
discussing, practising and getting feedback, rather than just listening.

My goal is to help students build a practical understanding of the subject, confidence and
critical thinking. In geospatial science and remote sensing, that means learning to work
with data, recognise uncertainty, justify their choices, and explain results clearly and
honestly.

**Clear structure and expectations.** Students make the most progress when tasks are clearly
defined and the steps are laid out. In a lab I start with the objectives, what success looks
like and why the exercise matters. In technical work a small misunderstanding at the start
can derail a whole session, so I set out key assumptions and common errors early.

**Engagement.** Engagement is one of the hardest parts of teaching, especially in lectures. I
break lectures into 10 to 15 minute sections with short activities, such as quick
multiple-choice questions, open questions and think-pair-share. They help students
understand the material and show me where they are confused, so I can adjust.

**A safe and inclusive environment.** Many students do not ask questions because they worry
about being judged. As someone from Latin America who speaks English as a second language, I
know that language and confidence can affect participation even when students are fully
capable. I use clear language, give written and spoken instructions, allow time to think,
and avoid assuming prior knowledge or a shared cultural background.

**Real skills.** In geospatial work the challenge is not pressing the right buttons but making
informed decisions with imperfect data and explaining the results responsibly. In my labs I
teach students to check data quality, spot common errors and understand how their choices
affect outcomes. My background in outdoor and sea-kayak instruction supports this, because
good performance comes from clear decisions, awareness of risk and the ability to adapt.

**AI.** Generative AI is changing how students study, write and code. I see it as a helpful
tool, not a replacement for creativity or critical thinking. I encourage students to use it
responsibly for brainstorming, debugging and explaining concepts, and to evaluate its output
critically. My assessments call for original decisions, real data and honest reasoning about
uncertainty and ethics.

I keep improving my teaching through practice, reflection and peer feedback.

I am interested in teaching remote sensing data science, computer vision and applied machine
learning, Python programming and reproducible analytics, and polar regions.

## Courses (University of Canterbury) {#courses}

From 2020 to 2023 I was a teaching assistant, tutor and lab demonstrator in ANTA102, ANTA201,
GEOG323, GEOG312 and GISC406, running tutorials and labs, marking and supporting students.
I also tutored during my MSc in Brazil.

### Guest lectures {#guest-lectures}

- **ANTA201, since 2021:** "Polar Remote Sensing"; "Ice tongues in the Western Ross Sea"
- **GISC406, since 2022:** "The Psychedelic World of Interferograms"
- **GEOG208, since 2023:** "Introduction to SAR"; "The value of lidar in New Zealand"

## Schools and workshops {#schools}

### Second IEEE GRSS New Zealand Radar Remote Sensing School: SAR and GNSS-R {#radar-school-2026}

**15–17 April 2026** · University of Canterbury

I organised this three-day international school with the Geospatial Research Institute and
IEEE GRSS. I secured funding through the IEEE GRSS school funding system, planned the
schedule and contacted the lecturers. I also submitted a proposal to the IEEE GRSS
Distinguished Lecturer programme, which brought an additional international lecturer. There
were 30 participants from Fiji, Australia and New Zealand, including industry professionals,
postgraduates and lecturers. I taught two hands-on labs: Data Access for SAR and GNSS-R, and
Change Detection with SAR.

### New Zealand SAR Workshop and hackathon {#sar-workshop-2024}

**2024**

The New Zealand SAR Workshop was held on 4 September 2024: a one-day workshop that brought
together practitioners, industry and academia to talk about the future of radar remote
sensing in New Zealand. I was on the organising committee and coordinated the event. As an
outcome, the New Zealand Space Agency asked the organising committee for a
[report to the New Zealand Space Agency](reports.qmd#ref-gomezfell2024sarworkshop).

I was also on the organising committee of the New Zealand Space Mission Design Hackathon at
the University of Canterbury, run as part of the IEEE GRSS New Zealand Chapter. It brought
together students and early career researchers to work on applied space problems.

### Expedition cruise lecturing {#cruise-lectures}

In the 2023/24 and 2024/25 summers I gave public lectures on Norwegian Star voyages to South
America and Antarctica: four voyages with four lectures each, and about 300 people at each
talk. The talks were "The Southern Ocean", "Antarctic Sea-Ice", "How to conduct scientific
research in Antarctica?" and "The Darwin Range Glaciers".

## Supervision and mentoring {#supervision}

- I am part of the supervisory team of a PhD student studying fast ice and ice shelf interactions in McMurdo Sound.
- At the Waterways Centre I helped supervise two MSc students: one mapped the Ashley braided river floodplain, and the other identified hāpua with a CNN model.
- I supervised three honours students working on New Zealand glaciers with SAR data.
- In 2023 I mentored a secondary school student through the Adopt a Scientist programme at Lincoln High School.
